# About this practice

I am using this file to practise linear regression in R. I used a small sample dataset to understand simple regression, multiple regression, prediction and diagnostic plots.

The data in this exercise is created for practice. It is not real student data.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

# 1. Packages

I use `ggplot2` for graphs. Most of the regression functions are already available in base R.

```{r packages}
if (!"ggplot2" %in% rownames(installed.packages())) {
  install.packages("ggplot2")
}
library(ggplot2)
```

# 2. Prepare the practice data

`Marks` is the outcome I want to explain. `Study_Hours` and `Attendance` are possible predictors.

```{r prepare-data}
regression_data <- data.frame(
  Student = paste0("Student", 1:12),
  Study_Hours = c(1, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 4.5, 5, 6, 6.5, 7, 8, 9),
  Attendance = c(55, 60, 62, 65, 70, 72, 75, 80, 82, 85, 90, 95),
  Marks = c(42, 46, 50, 53, 58, 63, 65, 70, 74, 77, 83, 90)
)

regression_data
head(regression_data)
str(regression_data)
summary(regression_data)

# Check missing values in each column.
colSums(is.na(regression_data))
```

# 3. Explore the variables

I check the distributions and relationships before fitting a model.

```{r explore-numeric}
summary(regression_data[c("Study_Hours", "Attendance", "Marks")])
```

## 3.1 Study hours and marks

```{r study-hours-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(regression_data, aes(x = Study_Hours, y = Marks)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Study Hours and Marks",
    x = "Study Hours",
    y = "Marks"
  )
```

## 3.2 Attendance and marks

```{r attendance-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(regression_data, aes(x = Attendance, y = Marks)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Attendance and Marks",
    x = "Attendance (%)",
    y = "Marks"
  )
```

# 4. Correlation

Correlation measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two numeric variables. It ranges from -1 to +1.

- Positive correlation: the variables tend to increase together.
- Negative correlation: one tends to decrease as the other increases.
- Correlation near zero: little linear association.

Correlation does not prove that one variable causes another.

```{r correlation}
cor(
  regression_data$Study_Hours,
  regression_data$Marks,
  method = "pearson"
)

# Correlations among all numeric variables.
cor(regression_data[c("Study_Hours", "Attendance", "Marks")])
```

# 5. Simple linear regression

Simple linear regression uses one predictor. Here I predict Marks using Study_Hours.

The formula `Marks ~ Study_Hours` means:

- `Marks` is the response variable (Y).
- `Study_Hours` is the predictor variable (X).

```{r simple-model}
simple_model <- lm(
  Marks ~ Study_Hours,
  data = regression_data
)

summary(simple_model)
```

## 5.1 Understanding the coefficients

The intercept is the estimated mark when study hours are zero. The slope estimates the change in marks for one additional study hour, according to this model.

```{r simple-coefficients}
coef(simple_model)
```

I also check the fitted values and residuals. A residual is the observed value minus the fitted value.

```{r fitted-residuals}
regression_data$Fitted_Marks <- fitted(simple_model)
regression_data$Residuals <- residuals(simple_model)

regression_data[, c("Student", "Marks", "Fitted_Marks", "Residuals")]
```

## 5.2 Regression graph

The points show the observed marks. The line is the fitted linear relationship.

```{r simple-regression-graph, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(regression_data, aes(x = Study_Hours, y = Marks)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Simple Linear Regression",
    x = "Study Hours",
    y = "Marks"
  )
```

# 6. Making predictions

I use `predict()` to estimate marks for new study-hour values. The new data must use the same predictor name as the model.

```{r simple-prediction}
new_students <- data.frame(
  Study_Hours = c(3, 5, 7, 8)
)

predicted_marks <- predict(
  simple_model,
  newdata = new_students
)

data.frame(
  Study_Hours = new_students$Study_Hours,
  Predicted_Marks = as.numeric(predicted_marks)
)
```

I can request a confidence interval for the estimated mean response.

```{r confidence-interval}
predict(
  simple_model,
  newdata = new_students,
  interval = "confidence"
)
```

A prediction interval is wider because it estimates a range for an individual future observation.

```{r prediction-interval}
predict(
  simple_model,
  newdata = new_students,
  interval = "prediction"
)
```

# 7. Multiple linear regression

Multiple regression uses two or more predictors. Here I use Study_Hours and Attendance to predict Marks.

```{r multiple-model}
multiple_model <- lm(
  Marks ~ Study_Hours + Attendance,
  data = regression_data
)

summary(multiple_model)
coef(multiple_model)
```

I compare the R-squared values, but I do not choose a model using R-squared alone. I also need to consider assumptions, data quality, adjusted R-squared and the purpose of the analysis.

```{r compare-r-squared}
simple_summary <- summary(simple_model)
multiple_summary <- summary(multiple_model)

data.frame(
  Model = c("Simple regression", "Multiple regression"),
  R_Squared = c(
    simple_summary$r.squared,
    multiple_summary$r.squared
  ),
  Adjusted_R_Squared = c(
    simple_summary$adj.r.squared,
    multiple_summary$adj.r.squared
  ),
  Residual_Standard_Error = c(
    simple_summary$sigma,
    multiple_summary$sigma
  )
)
```

# 8. Prediction with multiple regression

For multiple regression, the new data must include all predictors used in the model.

```{r multiple-prediction}
new_data_multiple <- data.frame(
  Study_Hours = c(4, 6, 8),
  Attendance = c(70, 80, 90)
)

multiple_predictions <- predict(
  multiple_model,
  newdata = new_data_multiple
)

data.frame(
  new_data_multiple,
  Predicted_Marks = as.numeric(multiple_predictions)
)
```

# 9. Main linear regression assumptions

These are the four main assumptions I am reviewing.

1. **Linearity:** the relationship between predictors and response should be reasonably linear.
2. **Independence:** observations/errors should be independent. This depends on how the data was collected and ordered.
3. **Homoscedasticity:** residuals should have roughly constant variance across fitted values.
4. **Normality of residuals:** residuals should be approximately normally distributed for standard small-sample inference.

Diagnostic plots help me look for warning signs. They do not prove that an assumption is satisfied.

# 10. Diagnostic plots

The four standard diagnostic plots from `plot(lm_model)` are:

1. **Residuals vs Fitted:** checks linearity and whether residual spread is roughly constant.
2. **Normal Q-Q:** checks whether residuals are approximately normal.
3. **Scale-Location:** another check of constant residual spread.
4. **Residuals vs Leverage:** helps identify observations that may have strong influence.

```{r diagnostic-plots, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(simple_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

These plots do not prove independence. I also need to consider how the observations were collected.

# 11. Checking residual normality

I use a histogram and Q-Q plot to inspect the residual distribution.

```{r residual-histogram, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
model_residuals <- residuals(simple_model)

hist(
  model_residuals,
  main = "Histogram of Regression Residuals",
  xlab = "Residuals",
  col = "lightblue",
  border = "white"
)
```

```{r residual-qq, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
qqnorm(model_residuals)
qqline(model_residuals, col = "red")
```

I can also run the Shapiro-Wilk test. Its null hypothesis is that the data are consistent with a normal distribution. I interpret the p-value together with the Q-Q plot, not by itself.

```{r shapiro-test}
shapiro.test(model_residuals)
```

# 12. Checking constant variance

I plot residuals against fitted values. I look for a roughly even vertical spread around zero.

```{r residuals-vs-fitted, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
plot(
  fitted(simple_model),
  residuals(simple_model),
  main = "Residuals vs Fitted Values",
  xlab = "Fitted Values",
  ylab = "Residuals",
  pch = 19
)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

# 13. Checking influential observations

Cook's distance helps identify observations that may strongly influence the fitted model. The reference line below is only a screening guide, not an automatic rule for deleting observations.

```{r cooks-distance, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
cook_values <- cooks.distance(simple_model)
cook_values

plot(
  cook_values,
  type = "h",
  main = "Cook's Distance",
  xlab = "Observation",
  ylab = "Cook's Distance"
)

abline(
  h = 4 / nrow(regression_data),
  lty = 2,
  col = "red"
)
```

# 14. Practice questions

I will try these questions after reviewing the examples.

1. Fit a simple model using Attendance to predict Marks.
2. Explain the intercept and slope from the simple model.
3. Use `predict()` to estimate marks for 5 study hours.
4. Fit a multiple regression model using Study_Hours and Attendance.
5. Explain R-squared and adjusted R-squared.
6. What is the difference between a confidence interval and a prediction interval?
7. Use `plot(simple_model)` and explain the four plots.
8. What pattern in Residuals vs Fitted may suggest non-linearity or unequal variance?
9. Why does correlation not prove causation?
10. Explain why I should not automatically remove an observation just because Cook's distance is high.

# My short summary

- Simple linear regression uses one predictor.
- Multiple linear regression uses two or more predictors.
- `lm()` fits a linear regression model.
- `summary()` displays the model results.
- `coef()` extracts the estimated coefficients.
- `predict()` makes predictions for new data.
- Residuals are observed values minus fitted values.
- Diagnostic plots help me check regression assumptions.
